open_questions.q: Why do so many flowers have 5 petals?
open_questions.why_open: A very large number of plants make flowers with 5 petals. Scientists know some of how a bud sets out its parts. They do not have one agreed answer for why five turns up so often.

open_questions.q: How exactly does a tiger get stripes?
open_questions.why_open: In 1952 the mathematician Alan Turing suggested that two chemicals spreading through the skin of a baby animal could make stripes and spots. In 2012 scientists found a pattern made this way in the mouths of mice. Nobody has yet shown it fully for a tiger.

Scientists have argued about this for more than a hundred years. One idea with good tests behind it is that stripes keep biting flies away. Other scientists think stripes help with heat, or with hiding. The argument is not over.

open_questions.q: Do bees enjoy looking at matching halves, as many people do?
open_questions.why_open: Trained bees can pick out shapes with matching halves. Nobody knows what that is like for a bee.

ask_kids: How many legs does that fly have? How could we count them when the fly will not sit still?
Look at your face in a steel plate. Do your two halves match exactly? Where do they differ?
How many pieces are inside this orange? Guess before we peel it.
Is that a spider or an insect? How can you tell without touching?
Where does the spiral on this murukku start? How many times does it go round?
Could you pick out our street's dog from a photo of ten dogs? What would you look for?

maths.problem: An ant has 3 legs on the left side. The two sides match. How many legs does the ant have in all?
maths.explain: The right side matches the left, so it has 3 legs too. 3 and 3 make 6. So the ant has 6 legs.
maths.context: In the game Six, Eight, Ten you gave each animal the same number of legs on both sides. This problem uses the same idea.
maths.why_maths: When two halves match, you count one half and double it. That is quicker than counting every leg on a moving ant.

maths.problem: Two ants and one spider are on the wall. How many legs are on the wall?
maths.explain: Each ant has 6 legs, and 6 and 6 make 12. The spider has 8 legs. Count on 8 from 12: 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20. So there are 20 legs.
maths.context: In the game Six, Eight, Ten you learned that an ant has 6 legs and a spider has 8. This problem puts three animals together.
maths.why_maths: If you know each animal's number, you can find the total without seeing a single leg.

maths.problem: You put 5 hibiscus flowers in a bowl of water. Each flower has 5 petals. How many petals are in the bowl?
maths.explain: Count in fives, once for each flower: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25. So there are 25 petals.
maths.context: In the Petal Count you found that a hibiscus keeps to 5 petals. This problem uses that to count many petals quickly.
maths.why_maths: Because every hibiscus has the same number, you can count in fives. You do not need to touch every petal.

maths.problem: A hibiscus has 5 petals. You count round the flower and get 7. How many petals did you count twice?
maths.explain: You said 7 numbers, but there are only 5 petals. 7 is 2 more than 5. So 2 petals were counted twice, most likely because the first petal was not marked.
maths.context: In the Petal Count you marked one petal before counting round the ring. This problem shows what happens without the mark.
maths.why_maths: Comparing your count with the number you expect helps you catch your own mistake and see how big it was.

maths.problem: A small animal on the wall has 4 legs on each side. Is this animal an insect? How do you know?
maths.answer: No. The animal has 8 legs, so they are not an insect. They may be a spider.
maths.explain: 4 and 4 make 8. An insect has 6 legs, and 8 is 2 more than 6. So this animal is not an insect.
maths.context: In the game Six, Eight, Ten you drew 6 legs for an ant and 8 for a spider. This problem uses those numbers to decide what an animal is.
maths.why_maths: The name 'insect' comes with a number in the rule. Adding the two sides and comparing with 6 tells you whether the animal fits the name.

roots.context: We cut vegetables, folded leaves, and counted legs and petals. Now let us think about who made these patterns.

deep_truth.truth: In Cut and Count, you counted the ridges on a lady's finger, and then the seed rooms inside. The two numbers were the same. The plant kept to one number, outside and inside, and never said a number word. So patterns with numbers in them are older than people. The plant made the five, and you gave the five a name.
deep_truth.habit: We think maths begins with people, in school and in books. But a lady's finger keeps to a number without one number word. An ant has 6 legs whether or not anyone counts them.
deep_truth.evidence: In Cut and Count, the ridges outside a lady's finger and the seed rooms inside gave the same number. In the Petal Count, two flowers of the same kind had the same number of petals.

three.who_am_i: You have two eyes, two ears, two hands and ten fingers. Your left side nearly matches your right side. You are a pattern too. You are also the one who notices patterns.
three.what_is_life: A plant sets out petals in a ring. A snail builds a spiral, a little at a time. Living things make patterns as they grow.
three.what_is_this_world: A snail shell is a spiral. A big storm seen from space is a spiral. Our galaxy, the Milky Way, is a spiral of stars. The same shape turns up in tiny things and in huge things.

roots.thread: A lady's finger starts as one tiny bud. As the bud grows, the parts form in a ring. A snail starts with one tiny shell and adds to the open edge, turn after turn. One small start, done again and again, becomes a pattern that you can count.

teachings.teaching: A father, Uddalaka, asks his son Shvetaketu to break open a banyan fruit, and then one of its tiny seeds. The son sees nothing inside the seed. The father says the whole great tree grows from that part, too fine to see.
teachings.link: You also cut a fruit open to look inside. You found seeds in a ring of rooms. Whatever sets out that ring is inside the seed, too small for your eyes.

teachings.teaching: Thiruvalluvar, the Tamil poet, says: whatever a thing is, and whatever kind it is, wisdom is to see what it truly is.
teachings.link: A spider looks like an insect until you count the legs. Looking closely and counting is one way to see what a thing truly is.

teachings.source: Galileo, The Assayer (Il Saggiatore), 1623, pages 237-238 in Stillman Drake's 1957 English translation
teachings.teaching: Galileo, an Italian scientist, wrote that the universe is like a great book written in the language of mathematics. He said its letters are triangles, circles and other shapes.
teachings.link: He meant that shapes and numbers are in the world already, and people learn to read them. The spiral was in the shell before anyone drew one. Not everyone agrees with him.

science.text: In 1996, scientists trained honeybees to choose shapes with two matching halves. The bees then chose new matching-halves shapes that they had never seen (Giurfa, Eichmann and Menzel, 1996). So people are not the only animals who can pick out this pattern.
How does a growing bud end up with exactly 5 petals, flower after flower? Scientists know parts of the answer, but not all of it.

other_view.view: They say the lady's finger is not doing maths. The bud grows five parts because of the way a bud grows, as water runs downhill because of the way water moves. They say maths begins only when someone counts, checks, and knows that five is five. So the pattern belongs to the plant, and the maths belongs to us.

practice.title: One leaf, one minute
practice.say: Hold one leaf in your open hand. Sit still and look at the leaf for one whole minute. Look at the edge. Look at the middle line. Look at the small lines that branch off. Now close your eyes. Can you still see the leaf? Open your eyes. What did you notice that you had never seen before?
practice.kid: Hold one leaf in your hand. Look at the leaf for one minute. Look at the edge and the lines. Close your eyes. Can you still see the leaf?

how_we_found_out.context: How do people count tigers in a forest, when tigers hide and all look alike at first? This card tells the true story of how the answer was found in India.
how_we_found_out.story: For many years, forest staff in India counted tigers by their paw prints, called pugmarks. A forester named S. R. Choudhury began this method in 1966. People believed that each tiger's paw print was different enough to tell the tigers apart. In the early 1990s a scientist from Karnataka, Ullas Karanth, tried another way in the Nagarahole forest. He fixed cameras beside the forest paths. A tiger who walked past set off the camera and took their own photo. Karanth looked at the stripes. No two tigers had the same stripes, so he could tell the tigers apart and count them. He published this work in 1995. Karanth and others also tested the paw print method on tigers in zoos, where the true number was known. People who studied the same set of prints gave answers from 8 tigers to 23 tigers. So paw prints could not be trusted. From 2006, India's national tiger count has used camera photos and stripes.
how_we_found_out.who: Ullas Karanth, and before him S. R. Choudhury
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People believed that each tiger could be told apart by paw prints. A test with zoo tigers showed this was wrong. People looking at the same prints gave answers from 8 tigers to 23.

Tiger flanks: the stripe patterns on the left and right sides of one tiger differ, so camera traps are set in pairs (standard practice in camera-trap studies of tigers).
Gastropod shells grow by adding new shell at the edge of the opening, so the oldest turns are at the tip (standard malacology).

Okra (Abelmoschus esculentus): five carpels and a pod with a five-sided cross-section in the common kinds (Go Botany, Native Plant Trust). Banana: the fruit comes from an ovary of three joined parts, and a cross-section shows three (university botany course notes).
Marigold and sunflower heads are made of many small flowers called florets (standard botany of the daisy family).
Ladybird spots do not show age: the number is fixed for the kind of ladybird (Forest Preserve District of Will County, and other naturalist sources).
